blocks: Coffee does not give you energy. It hides how tired you are. Here is the trick, one molecule at a time.
Every hour you are awake, your brain burns fuel and leaves behind a molecule called adenosine. It builds up all day.
Adenosine docks onto receptors in your brain. The more of them it fills, the heavier your eyes get. Scientists call it sleep pressure.
Caffeine is shaped almost exactly like adenosine. It slips into the same receptors, but it does not switch them on. It just takes the seat.
The tiredness signal cannot get through, so you feel alert. It usually kicks in within thirty to sixty minutes.
But adenosine keeps piling up behind the blockade. When the caffeine wears off, it lands all at once. That is the crash.

Your body clears about half of it in roughly five hours, so an afternoon coffee is still working at bedtime. For most healthy adults, up to four hundred milligrams a day, about four cups, is considered safe.
